{{Short description|American environmental activist}}
{{use mdy dates|date=October 2024}}
'''Charles Frederick Wurster Jr.''' (August 1, 1930 – July 6, 2023) was an American biochemist and environmental activist who was one of the founders of the [[Environmental Defense Fund]] (EDF) who were instrumental in the initiation of [[environmental law]] and legal action against the use of [[DDT]].<ref name=WaPo>{{cite news|author=Diamond, Dan|title=Charles Wurster, scientist who battled to ban pesticide DDT, dies at 92|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2023/07/25/charles-wurster-environmental-defense-fund-dead/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=July 25, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.haverford.edu/college-communications/news/qa-charles-f-wurster-52 |title=Leading the Fight Against DDT: Charles F. Wurster '52 |date=December 2015 |website=News, Haverford College}} (interview by Cat Lazaroff)</ref> He was a professor emeritus at [[Stony Brook University]].

==Education and career==
A native Philadelphian, Wurster grew up in [[Olney, Philadelphia]].<ref name=Inquirer>{{cite news|author=Miles, Gary|url=https://www.inquirer.com/obituaries/charles-wurster-obituary-edf-philadelphia-stony-brook-environment-20230719.html |title=Charles F. Wurster, environmental pioneer and science professor emeritus, has died at 92 |date=19 July 2023 |newspaper=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]}}</ref> He began his lifelong involvement in birdwatching when he was a teenager in high school.<ref name=Newsday/> After high school education at [[Germantown Friends School]], he graduated in 1952 with a bachelor's degree in chemistry from [[Haverford College]].<ref name=Newsday>{{cite news|author=Winslow, Olivia|url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/obituaries/charles-wurster-obituary-g39lmhz0 |title=Charles Wurster, Stony Brook University professor, dies at 92 |date=3 August 2023 |newspaper=Newsday}}</ref> One summer during his youth, he worked in an Alaskan gold mine.<ref name=Inquirer/> After earning a master's degree in organic chemistry from the [[University of Delaware]] in 1954, he graduated in 1957 with a Ph.D. in organic chemistry from [[Stanford University]].<ref name=Newsday/> His thesis advisor was [[Harry Stone Mosher]].<ref>{{cite thesis|url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/2188284 |title=The thermal decomposition of primary hydroperoxides |date=1957 |last1=Wurster |first1=Charles Frederick }} (catalog entry for Ph.D. thesis)</ref> For the academic year 1957–58, Wurster was a [[Fulbright Fellow]] in [[Innsbruck, Austria]]. Wurster was employed from 1959 to 1962 as a researcher by [[Monsanto]] and from 1962 to 1965 as a postdoctoral research at [[Dartmouth College]].<ref name=Newsday/> At [[Stony Brook University]] (SBU), he became an assistant professor in 1965 and retired in 1994 as professor emeritus in SBU's School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences. In 2009, SBU awarded him an honorary degree.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.stonybrook.edu/university/sbu-environmentalist-charles-f-wurster-co-founder-of-environmental-defense-fund-dies-at-92/ |title=SBU Environmentalist Charles F. Wurster, Co-Founder of Environmental Defense Fund, Dies at 92 - SBU News |date=3 August 2023 |website=News, Stony Brook University}}</ref> He was a visiting professor in Australia, Norway, and South Korea.<ref name=Inquirer/>

In 2015, [[Oxford University Press]] published Wurster's book about the DDT struggles during the 1960s and 1970s.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BrC6BwAAQBAJ | title=DDT Wars: Rescuing Our National Bird, Preventing Cancer, and Creating the Environmental Defense Fund | isbn=978-0-19-021941-3 | last1=Wurster | first1=Charles F. | date=2015 | publisher=Oxford University Press }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1093/biosci/biw021 |title=Setting the Record Straight on DDT {review of ''DDT Wars'' by Charles F. Wurster)|date=2016 |last1=Conis |first1=Elena |author-link=Elena Conis |journal=BioScience |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=329–331 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Armistead, Henry T.|url=https://blog.aba.org/2016/06/character-assassination-slander-and-ddt-science.html |title=Character Assassination, Slander, and DDT Science (review of ''DDT Wars'' by Charles F. Wurster) |website=American Birding Association |date=30 June 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Arnold, Melissa|url=https://tbrnewsmedia.com/book-review-ddt-wars-by-charles-f-wurster/ |title=Book Review: 'DDT Wars' by Charles F. Wurster &#124; TBR News Media |date=7 October 2016 }}</ref>

==Research, environmental activism, and public education==
The research of Wurster and his collaborators provided scientific evidence for the environmental dangers caused by [[chlorinated hydrocarbon]] [[insecticide]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://you.stonybrook.edu/somas/2019/09/30/the-modern-environmental-movement-was-born-here-as-part-of-marine-sciences-at-stony-brook-university/ |title=The Modern Environmental Movement Was Born Here as part of Marine Sciences at Stony Brook University |date=30 September 2019 }}</ref> He participated in, and reported on, government hearings that resulted in various bans against the use of DDT.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.2307/1294792|jstor=1294792 |last1=Wurster |first1=Charles F. |title=DDT Goes to Trial in Madison |journal=BioScience |date=1969 |volume=19 |issue=9 |pages=809–813 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1093/bioscience/23.2.105 |title=DDT Proved Neither Essential nor Safe |date=1973 |last1=Wurster |first1=C. F. |journal=BioScience |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=105–106 }}</ref> After DDT bans prompted by groups such as the EDF, many bird species quickly recovered.<ref>{{cite web|title=DDT and Birds|author=Ehrlich, Paul R.|author-link=Paul R. Ehrlich|author2=Dobkin, David S.|author3=Wheye, Darryl|website=web.stanford.edu|url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/stanfordbirds/text/essays/DDT_and_Birds.html}} [https://law.lclark.edu/programs/environmental_and_natural_resources_law/faculty_and_staff/Adjuncts/daviddobkin.php David Dobkin]; [https://artist-registry.stanford.edu/html/Wheye.html Darryl Wheye]</ref>

A 1969 paper on DDT residues in connection with [[fiddler crab]]s was coauthored by Wurster, [[George M. Woodwell]], and William E. Odum<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1126/science.164.3879.576 |title=DDT Residues Absorbed from Organic Detritus by Fiddler Crabs |date=1969 |last1=Odum |first1=W. E. |last2=Woodwell |first2=G. M. |last3=Wurster |first3=C. F. |journal=Science |volume=164 |issue=3879 |pages=576–577 |pmid=17792341 |bibcode=1969Sci...164..576O }}</ref> (who was the first son of [[Eugene Odum]]).<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AsNJZpXQVCMC&pg=PA134 | title=Eugene Odum: Ecosystem Ecologist and Environmentalist | isbn=978-0-8203-2473-9 | last1=Craige | first1=Betty Jean | date=2002 | publisher=University of Georgia Press |page=134}}</ref>

In 1976 Wurster and [[Art Cooley|Arthur P. Cooley]] suggested that, in many high school and college courses, students' writing of term papers might be replaced by students' writing of petitions. Such petitions to federal, state, or local governments might request changes in policies with environmentally harmful consequences. Wurster and Cooley argued that motivation of students can be enhanced by real-world projects — furthermore, writing petitions can teach the students about their rights and responsibilities as citizens and how to participate in government.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.2307/1297427|jstor=1297427 |last1=Wurster |first1=Charles F. |last2=Cooley |first2=Arthur P. |title=An Alternative to Term Papers |journal=BioScience |date=1976 |volume=26 |issue=8 |page=477 }}</ref>

Wurster had many collaborators for his numerous scientific articles. R. George Rowland (1941–1990) was often one of Wurster's coauthors.<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam|website=Stony Brook University|date=February 2017 |url=https://you.stonybrook.edu/somas/people/in-memoriam/}}</ref> In 1984, Wurster, Rowland, and Paul Lundy published a marine algal [[bioassay]] for detecting toxic chemical pollutants.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0043-1354(84)90068-X |title=A two-species marine algal bioassay for detecting aquatic toxicity of chemical pollutants |date=1984 |last1=Lundy |first1=Paul |last2=Wurster |first2=Charles F. |last3=Rowland |first3=R.George |journal=Water Research |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=187–194 |bibcode=1984WatRe..18..187L }}</ref>

Wurster was a world class birder and leader for ornithology and ecology tours in the Arctic, Antarctic, Africa, and South America. He made an appearance in the [[Nova (American TV program)|NOVA]] television documentary ''Return of the Osprey'', originally broadcast in the United States on March 18, 1986.<ref name=Inquirer/><ref>{{cite web|title=NOVA TV Programs, January 1986 – January 1987|website=pbs.org/wgbh/nova/|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/listseason/13.html}}</ref>

Wurster served on EDF's board of trustees for over 55 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.edf.org/remembering-pioneer-charles-wurster |title=Remembering pioneer Charles Wurster |date=10 July 2023 |website=Environmental Defense Fund (edf.org)}}</ref> He also helped to establish the [[Environmental Defence Society]] in New Zealand and served on the board of trustees of the [[Defenders of Wildlife]].<ref name=Inquirer/>

==Death==
A lifelong [[Asthma|asthmatic]] who never smoked, Wurster died at his daughter's home in [[Arlington County, Virginia|Arlington, Virginia]], from [[chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] (COPD).<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/07/21/metro/charles-wuster-environmentalist-cofounded-edf-save-birds-from-ddt-dies/ |title=Charles Wurster's fight of a lifetime: Defending the environment, saving the birds |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |date=July 21, 2023}}</ref><ref name=Newsday/>

==Family==
Wurster's first wife was Dorothy Hadley Burster-Hill (1932–2007), a cytogeneticist,<ref name=obitWurster-Hill/> an authority on the chromosomes of carnivores,<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF00336201 |title=Comparative cytogenetic studies in the order carnivora |date=1968 |last1=Wurster |first1=D. H. |last2=Benirschke |first2=K. |journal=Chromosoma |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=336–382 |pmid=5708272 }}</ref> and a faculty member in the Dartmouth Medical School's department of pathology. Before their divorce, Charles and Doris Wurster had a son Steven,<ref name=obitWurster-Hill>{{cite journal|doi=10.1159/000109610 |title=Doris H. Wurster-Hill (1932–2007) |date=2007 |last1=Ward |first1=Oscar G. |last2=Brothman |first2=Arthur R. |journal=Cytogenetic and Genome Research |volume=119 |issue=1–2 |page=1 }}</ref> who became a woodworker living in [[McCall, Idaho]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bber.umt.edu/ID/detail.asp?prodParam=&cName=McCall+Woodworks&facilitycode=2505 | title=Idaho Wood Products Directory - Detail page }}</ref> Wurster's second wife was Eva Tank-Nielsen, a Norwegian diplomat. Before their divorce, they had a son Erik and a daughter Nina.<ref name=Newsday/> Nina Wurster made her career in healthcare, but she and her children participate as volunteers for EcoAction Arlington.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ecoactionarlington.org/about-us/staff-and-board/|title=EcoAction Arlington Team members|website=www.ecoactionarlington.org}}</ref> Erik Wurster became an expert in promoting sustainable energy projects.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://theorg.com/org/biolite/org-chart/erik-wurster|title=Erik Wurster - Vp, Environmental Markets And Sustainability at BioLite|website=The Org}}</ref> When Wurster died at age 92 in 2023, he was survived by his three children, four grandchildren, and his longtime companion Marie Gladwish,<ref name=Newsday/> an artist and world traveler.<ref>{{cite web|author=Pizzi, Donna|url=https://www.portraitmagazine.com/orcas-island-gary-gladwish |title=Living with the Land | website=portraitmagazine.com}}</ref>
